title: Building trust in AI-driven finance
full_text:
Many finance teams have been reluctant to embrace artificial intelligence, cognisant of the inherent risks, while also curious about the tech's potential to transform and automate. With the right partner, CFOs can get the best from AI, control external factors and maintain superior governance standards.
Amendra Pratap, who previously worked at Macquarie, is the founder and managing director of Octane Software Solutions, an IBM Gold Partner, which has been recognised in The Australian Financial Review's Fast Lists 2026.
The firm, which is celebrating its 10th anniversary, manages budgeting, forecasting, analytics and financial reporting for large corporations including airline Fiji Airways, auto parts firm MyCar Tyre & Auto, media company News Corp, appliance firm Rinnai, fintech Shift Financial, financial services firm Tyro and tech firm WiseTech. Global clients include Emaar Properties in Dubai.
"Octane is a specialist finance technology firm with teams in Australia and India. Our people are world-class experts," says Pratap, who is an IBM champion, along with two of his colleagues.
Octane partners with tech firms Anthropic, AWS, IBM and Microsoft, with its products built on their platforms. The Octane culture supports the firm's growth.
"We treat our customers very well and we treat our employees even better. That means we have very low turnover in our teams, including in our Indian business," says Pratap. "We do well thanks to the quality of the work we do, the warm embrace we give clients and the expertise we bring."
One innovation is a fractional support model called Octane Blue that clients can dial up or down. "We provide a fixed-price service across any tool we offer, so clients have access to support partners for all their applications," he adds.
Artificial intelligence offers many opportunities for finance teams to automate manual processes. This means CFOs can partner more effectively with the broader business through providing insights and guidance, instead of being in the back office doing process work. But this cannot come at the cost of governance.
"Finance is the one department that cannot afford to have its numbers wrong, because the figures are audited and analysed, especially if the business is a listed entity," says Pratap. "There's an additional layer of scrutiny not just on the numbers, but also on the forecast. Public companies have to defend and hit their forecast, otherwise they will be punished by the market."
The key is for finance teams to work with partners such as Octane, who understand the underlying technology and can verify AI's output.
"AI in some forms can be unreliable. It won't give you the same answer twice and it will make up things. We implement AI in a governed fashion, where everything we do is traceable and auditable. That allows finance teams to automate processes and use AI without compromising governance."
Octane's model is a significant point of difference. In some cases, finance teams may have started AI trials, only to come up against stumbling blocks around internal auditing. Octane's systems distinguish between data generated by AI and data generated by core transactional systems. Its underlying technology means finance teams always have an understanding of the logic behind the answers the tools produce.
"The apps we have developed over the past 12 months plug into our clients' source systems, with pre-built forecasting, accounts payable processing, budgeting and monthly or weekly reports," says Pratap. "Everything is designed to be traceable and auditable."
While businesses are exploring how to use AI to reduce expenses, it is vital to appreciate the cost of not rolling out the technology in the right way. "AI can reduce processing costs, but if the underlying governance is not there, the potential risks are just too high," he says.
Octane's tools are built using IBM's enterprise-grade platforms, IBM watsonx and IBM Planning Analytics. IBM can host the data in Australia and does not train its models on client data. Octane limits the tasks its AI agents can perform and there is always a human in the loop when exceptions or discrepancies are identified. To help control costs, IBM uses messaging instead of tokens.
"We can trace each action an agent performs and when a human has interacted with the system and applied external knowledge to come to an outcome," says Pratap. "Doing this reduces the risk of hallucinations, so the AI is very contained. Everything is grounded in the client's source system, so there is always a single source of truth."
